quotes.text: After spending years playing the Midwestern bar circuit, Cheap Trick came roaring out of Rockford, Ill. in 1977 with a sound that was equal parts Beatlemania, heavy metal, Who-like power chording, and Badfinger/Rasperries power-pop sheen.

Guitarist Rick Neilsen did most of the songwriting and wrenched this messy, hooky, garbagey, completely over the top racket that you'd never believe could come out a skinny baseball cap-wearing weirdo who looked like he just rode his bicycle from his day job delivering newspapers.
Bassist Tom Petersson must have listened to his old Move records daily, as he churned out this incredibly deep bass thrust that made him and Carlos a rythm section that stomped like a Brontasauras.
Add a warped, sinister sense of humor - they sang songs about pedophiles, barbituites, suicide, and celebrity serial killers - and you've got a winning combination.

Cheap Trick tighten their attack and write more pop for an approach that's a couple of leagues in quality above the debut, which had lots of great noise but was kind of hit-and-miss in regards to melody.
I prefer the pop sheen of this disc... otherwise it's as close to perfection as pop-metal/power-pop gets.
"Big Eyes" rests on this monstrously catchy Nielsen/Petersson riff that goes haywire in the stunning midsection.
Their Beatles influences, pop-punk style was all their own. You heard a Cheap Trick song, you basically knew it was a Cheap Trick song.
Rick's crazy guitars weren't to make up for the fact he can't play because he sure as hell can as he filled every album with some great solos and killer riffs.
Tom Petersson's bassline was the driving force behind the rhythm section and with Bun E Carlos on drums, that rhythm section was pretty freakin' tight.

Thanks to the production by Tony Platt, Cheap Trick came out with an album that had no balls and sounded so dated with the massive keyboards that you just throw your hands up in the air and say "what is this crap". It was someone who's vision for the band that does not fit the band.

Jack Douglas might have had a vision of a much rawer and edgier Cheap Trick, but Tony Platt's mix and Mark Radice's song writing and keyboards really wimped it out and lost any passion or even Cheap Trick out of it.
They brought their sound in to the new millennium and still had a little of that old Cheap Trick sound, but it is still missing enough of the old to make people care.
As strange as I though this might be with Rundgren on the boards, I was pleasantly surprised that Cheap Trick was Cheap Trick on the album and they didn't stray too far down any weird path.
Cheap Trick had helped invent a form of trashy rock theatrics that were colonizing the pop charts in the late '80s, but the band hadn't been able to take advantage of that.
"The Flame" is a thoroughly average song, and it can't touch the freewheeling melodic brightness and outsized personality of Cheap Trick's best music.

Cheap Trick's early albums were some of the sharpest, brightest arena rock to come out of of the '70s. The band didn't play punk or new wave, but they liked punk and new wave, and you can hear distant echoes of those sounds in their juiced-up, efficient power-pop ragers. There's also an early-Beatles sense of excitement.
